title: Mechanisms of Microbial Pathogenesis
lead: This chapter explores microbial pathogenesis (Greek: patho- disease, genesis- birth of), or how microbes cause disease. The scope of this topic is quite broad, so only a concise overview can be presented in a chapter like this. The chapter begins with an overview of the viral replication cycle, followed by the mechanisms of pathogenesis of viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic pathogens.

blocks.text: Viruses cannot synthesize ATP or conduct major anabolic reactions. Therefore, viruses must infect host cells and utilize the cell’s biosynthetic machinery. In the process, some viruses kill the host cell, some use the host cell or the host cell’s genome as their residence, and some turn the host cell into a tumor. The virus’s effects on host cells and the immune system’s responses to viral infection constitute the signs of viral pathogenesis.

Understanding the virus replication cycle helps explain viral pathogenesis. Max Delbrück (1906-1981) observed in the 1930s that when a few viruses capable of causing infection are mixed with some host cells, the viruses temporarily disappear. No virus can be recovered from the mixture for a while. This period is called the eclipse. However, a few tens of minutes later, a very large number of viruses emerge. The number of virions produced per infected cell is called the burst size. The virus counts plateau once the last live host cell is infected and killed.

Delbrück termed this phenomenon the one-step growth curve (Fig. 11.1). This observation indicated that viruses do not divide like a cell; instead, the viral replication cycle involves synthesizing viral molecules and assembling them to produce many new virus particles. The virus replication cycle typically encompasses six steps: attachment, penetration, uncoating, biosynthesis, assembly, and egress (Fig. 11.1). All these steps except attachment and egress are completed during the eclipse period.

particles can’t be recovered during the eclipse period. Many virions emerged after the eclipse period, but the count plateaus, indicating a one-step growth. B. Virus replication cycle. The six steps of the cycle are shown.

blocks.text: Attachment

Attachment is the binding of certain surface molecules of a virus particle (ligands) with certain surface molecules of the host cell (receptors) (Fig. 11.2). Receptor-ligand binding is a lock-and-key-like interaction. A virus can infect only the cells that have its receptors. It defines the host range (host species the virus can infect) and tissue tropism (the specific cells of the host organism the virus can infect). A virus cannot infect a cell lacking receptors for it. No known bacterial or plant viruses infect human cells because of host range limitations. A virus is dermatotropic, pneumotropic, viscerotropic, or neurotropic if it can infect the integumentary system, respiratory system, internal organs, or nervous system. Those organs have the receptors for the virus in question.
Penetration

Penetration is an active (i.e., energy-dependent) transportation of the receptor-bound viruses inside the host cell. Bacterial and fungal cells have a thick cell wall. Viruses that infect those cells have enzymes that make a hole in the cell wall through which the viruses inject their genome directly into the host cell. Thus, bacterial and fungal viruses penetrate and uncoat at the same time.

Animal viruses may penetrate in two different ways. Some enveloped viruses penetrate by fusing their envelope with the plasma membrane and releasing the capsid inside the cytoplasm of the cell (Fig. 11.2). The receptor-ligand interactions allow such membrane fusion. Naked viruses and some enveloped viruses enter cells via receptor-mediated endocytosis. The virus enters the host cell in a clathrin-coated endosome (see Chapter 9).
Fig. 11.2. The attachment, penetration, and uncoating steps of HIV-1. A. Attachment and penetration. The virus

ligand gp120 binds the host cell receptors CD4 and CCR5 (1 and 2). The binding interactions cause the virus’s envelope to fuse with the plasma membrane of the host cell (3). Actin and microtubules in the host cell move the virus capsid toward the nucleus (4 and 5). B. Uncoating. The capsid attaches to a nuclear pore complex (steps 5-6). The capsid then gradually disintegrates, releasing the genome (step 7), which completes the uncoating step. Uncoating Uncoating is a complete or partial disassembly of the envelope and the capsid. The acidic pH and enzymes in the endosome facilitate uncoating. DNA viruses usually uncoat in the nucleus, while RNA viruses may uncoat in the cytoplasm or the nucleus.
Biosynthesis

Biosynthesis is the synthesis of a virus molecule in the host cell. Depending on the virus species, biosynthesis can have five different steps: (a) replication of the viral genome, (b) transcription of the viral genes, (c) grooming of the viral mRNAs, (d) translation of the viral mRNAs, and (e) grooming of the viral proteins.

Processes of biosynthesis differ across virus species. The host cell supplies the raw materials (such as nucleotides and amino acids) for biosynthesis. However, the virus involved may supply some enzymes for genome replication, RNA transcription, and RNA and protein processing. For example, RNA viruses must have an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RDRP) to replicate and transcribe their RNA genomes, and retroviruses must have reverse transcriptase (RT) to synthesize cDNA (human cells lack such enzymes). Virus assembly

Much less is known about how viruses are assembled. The process could be as diverse as the virus species. The site of assembly varies by virus families. For example, herpesviruses assemble in the nucleus, whereas poxviruses assemble in the cytoplasm. Generally, the cellular membranes serve as the anchoring platform for viral assembly. The virus capsomeres (units that create the capsid, usually made of one or more coat proteins) unite by protein-protein interactions to form the capsid. The assembly process involves proteolytic processing of coat proteins, processing of the viral genome, and protein-protein and protein-nucleic acid interactions. In helical viruses, the capsomeres directly bind to the viral genome to form the nucleocapsid. For icosahedral viruses, the capsomeres create an initial capsid. The scaffold protein binds the genome and packs it inside the initial capsid.

The initially assembled virion may undergo maturation. During maturation, some of the capsid proteins are further processed by proteases. Many virus particles are assembled without a genome or other necessary components. Such virus particles are defective and incapable of infecting a host cell.
Viral egress

For enveloped viruses: The processes of virus assembly, maturation, and egress are coordinated. Virus egress is not well understood. Enveloped viruses bud out of the nuclear membrane and then the plasma membrane (example: herpes viruses) or the plasma membrane (example: influenza viruses). The viral envelope proteins are localized to patches on the cellular membrane, where host cell microtubules deliver the viral nucleocapsid. The interactions among the viral matrix protein, nucleocapsid proteins, and envelope glycoproteins help the enveloped virion detach from the cellular membrane (Fig. 11.4). This may leave a small hole in the plasma membrane that soon heals. Enveloped viruses usually do not kill the host cell; instead, they use it as a virus factory. However, the budding of many virions at once may leave too many tiny holes in the membrane for an extended period, killing the host cell.

For naked viruses: The process of egress of naked viruses is less well understood. Plant and bacterial naked viruses are cytopathic (they kill the host cell after completing the replication cycle). Once the host cell breaks open, the viruses egress. Some naked animal viruses, such as adenoviruses, egress after the collapse of the host cells. Some very naked animal viruses, such as poliovirus, may use a host cell’s microtubules to exit the cell before the cell's death.
Fig. 11.4. Assembly and egress of viruses. A. Assembly and egress of herpes simplex virus (an enveloped virus).

The virus’s capsid proteins are transported to the nucleus, where they bind the virus’s genomic DNA and form a capsid. The capsid buds out initially through the nuclear envelope and then through Golgi vesicles before egressing through the plasma membrane. B. Assembly and egress of the influenza virus. The viral envelope proteins assemble on the plasma membrane. The nucleocapsid assembles beneath the envelope proteins. As the virus buds from the plasma membrane, the viral HA protein may bind to sialic acid receptors on the host cell, but the viral NA protein cleaves sialic acid to allow the virus to move away from the dying host cell.

Permissive, semi-permissive and non-permissive cells A cell carrying viral receptors can be a permissive, semi-permissive, or non-permissive host cell. The infection process may have the following consequences on the host cells.

Permissive cells: They allow productive infection, including completion of the viral replication cycle and the generation of infectious progeny viruses. The cell may be killed by the process. Infection of a permissive cell usually leads to acute infection.

Semi-permissive cell: These cells support viral biosynthesis and progeny virus production, but the process is slow. Since the viral load remains low, the immune system may not respond adequately, leading to a chronic infection. Non-permissive cells: These cells do not support viral biosynthesis; thus, the infection is non-productive (i.e., no progeny virus is produced). However, tumor viruses encode oncoproteins that disrupt the cell cycle, causing cells to divide repeatedly. Tumor viruses may transform the non-permissive cells into semi-permissive cells and then into tumor cells.

blocks.text: A few viruses can cause disease using bacterial exotoxin-like proteins (see Section 11.2) without infecting the host cells. For example, certain rotaviruses, SARS-CoV-2, and HIV bind cell receptors and induce an inflammatory response. Most viruses cause disease by infecting host cells and replicating within them. The infected cells may die, change phenotype, or become tumor cells. Any of these events can affect the infected subject. Viruses may contain one or more virulence factors (Table 11.2), attributes that enhance their pathogenicity. The host organism's immune responses cause most disease pathologies. Some viral infections (for example, latent infections) may not show any clinical signs because the immune system does not respond to the virus during latency.
Table 11.2. Common virulence factors of pathogenic viruses.
Virulence factors How do the factors play out?

Fast replication Excessive viral replication commandeers the host’s synthetic machinery. It depletes the host cell's resources, which may ultimately lead to the host cell’s death (as observed with influenza viruses). Viral macromolecules may assemble into insoluble inclusion particles that precipitate inside the cell, causing toxicity.

Damaging enzymes Viral enzymes may destroy and/or modify host chromosomal DNA, RNA, and proteins, crippling the host cell's biosynthetic machinery (for example, an enzyme of poliovirus destroys the host cell's capped mRNAs).

Fusion glycoproteins The envelope glycoproteins of some viruses (respiratory syncytial virus, for example) cause several host cells to fuse and form a giant cell. The giant cells ultimately collapse, leaving a cavity inside the tissue.

Superantigens Some viruses (such as Epstein-Barr virus and SARS-CoV-2) have superantigens that bind CD4 of T cells along with the MHC II molecules or macrophages and excessively activate TH cells. The activated TH cells release excess cytokines, which induce various damaging inflammatory responses.

Toxic molecules Toxic molecules from viruses may affect host cells. For example, herpes simplex viruses produce Cowdry type A inclusion bodies in the infected cells, which kill the host cell; the NSP4 protein of rotavirus kills active intestinal epithelial cells, causing diarrhea.
Changes in size and shape of the host cells

In tissue culture, infected host cells (animal cells) become rounder and smaller. Cells that normally attach to the substratum (i.e., the plastic plate) may float in the culture medium due to detachment of their anchors (Fig. 11.5). Similar processes may occur in cells in infected tissues.

Cell lysis

A cytopathic virus kills the infected host cell. Cytopathic viruses produce enzymes that may destroy host proteins, RNA, or DNA, causing a host shutdown (sudden stop of normal cellular activities) and cell death. Some viruses produce insoluble inclusion bodies within infected cells, causing cell death (Fig. 11.5). Some enveloped viruses cause infected cells to fuse with neighboring cells, forming giant cells (Fig. 11.5) that ultimately collapse. Apoptotic cell death Ligands on some viruses (for example, HIV-1) bind host cell receptors and trigger an apoptotic signal. The cell undergoes apoptosis (the nucleus condenses and the cell breaks into small fragments) (Fig. 11.5). Cytotoxic activities Cytotoxic cells are host leucocytes that kill virus-infected host cells. Virus-infected cells display viral antigens on their MHC I molecules, which trigger TC cells to kill them. If antibodies bind to virus-infected cells, NK cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, and neutrophils bind the antibodies and kill the infected cells. This process is called antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC, see Chapter 9).
Virus-induced tumors

About 15% of all cancers detected worldwide are caused by viruses. Nearly 100% of the cases of cervical cancer are associated with human papillomavirus infections. Oncogenic viruses such as Epstein-Barr virus, Kaposi’s sarcoma virus, papillomavirus, and adenovirus have oncogenes (cancer-causing genes). Oncogenic viruses obtained viral oncogenes (i.e., v-oncogenes) from their host cells. Host cells have protooncogenes that encode proteins that affect the cell cycle, allowing the host cells to divide rapidly when necessary. Protooncogenes include genes for transcription regulators, growth factors, growth factor receptors, and signal-transducing proteins.

The cells tightly regulate the expression of the proto-oncogenes. However, mutations in the protooncogenes create cellular oncogenes (c-oncogenes). The cells can no longer regulate the expression of c-oncogenes. Proteins encoded by c-oncogenes transform the cell. The transformed cells replicate more frequently and create a cell mass, a tumor. Tumor cells appear like cells of the local tissue and remain in the same location. However, tumor cells accumulate more mutations and turn into cancer cells. Cancer cells do not appear like the local cells. They destroy tissue structure, cause more blood vessels to grow, and ultimately move away from the tissue into the blood and then to other organs. Some of the migrated cancer cells form new tumors in the organs they migrated to. This process is called metastasis. The oncoviruses have somehow obtained the c-oncogenes from their host cell in the evolutionary past. When oncoviruses infect non-permissive host cells, their v-oncogene transforms the host cell in a manner similar to c- oncogenes. The transformed cells become tumor cells and subsequently cancer cells. For example, human papillomavirus infection causes tumors (warts) of the skin and cancer of the cervix. Epstein-Barr virus infection of B cells causes lymphoma, while infection of endothelial cells by Kaposi’s sarcoma virus may lead to sarcoma (cancer of connective tissue). Although a very large fraction of some human populations is infected with the Epstein-Barr virus and Kaposi’s sarcoma virus, the immune system keeps the virus infections under control and prevents cancer. However, if an infected person develops severe immunodeficiency, they may develop cancers. About 10,000 cases of EBV-related lymphoma and cervical cancer caused by human papillomavirus are detected in the USA annually. All humans are repeatedly infected with human adenoviruses throughout their lifetimes. Although human adenoviruses may transform infected cells, they kill the cells to complete their replication cycle, preventing the formation of tumors. Some viruses, such as the hepatitis B and hepatitis C viruses, lack oncogenes yet can still cause cancers, especially when infections are chronic. Chronic infections are associated with chronic inflammation and the continuous production of cytokines. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) released by leukocytes during inflammation may mutate the DNA of some host cells. Some cytokines induce rapid cell division, which may lead to the accumulation of mutations in the genome and ultimately to cell transformation. The genomes of DNA viruses may integrate into the host chromosome, which can also lead to cell transformation and tumorigenesis.

Effects of virus infection on the host organisms Viruses enter the host body through injured skin, mucous membranes, or directly into the blood. The delivered viruses initially infect local cells and replicate there. The viral disease may not develop till the virus reaches and infects cells of the target tissues. For example, the rabies lyssavirus initially infects epithelial cells of the skin or the mucous membranes. Still, signs of disease appear only when the virus reaches the brain via neurons that innervate the initial sites of infection. The period between virus transmission and disease development is the incubation period, which may vary from days to months depending on the virus species. If the innate immune system clears the virus, no disease signs appear (this is a silent infection), or only minor signs appear. If the virus replicates and damages tissue, the adaptive immunity induces full-blown signs of the disease (Table 11.3). Disease signs resulting from the immune response are part of immunopathogenesis (see Chapter 9).
Table 11.3. Immunopathogenesis due to virus infections.
Cytokine release Fever, chills, and body pain, especially during the prodrome.
Superantigen effect Excessive TH cell activation and cytokine release may lead to severe inflammatory responses, including vascular shock.

Immune complex formation Weak IgG response to viral antigens may produce soluble immune complexes (i.e., virus antigen bound to antibodies) that may lead to type III hypersensitivity diseases (see Chapter 9).

Delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) T cell immune response to certain viral infections may cause severe DTH upon second and subsequent exposure to the same virus (as in dengue hemorrhagic fever, see Chapter 9).
Tissue damage Death of the infected cells, and imperfect repair of the affected tissues and organs (for example, liver cirrhosis after chronic hepatitis C virus infection).
Immunosuppression The virus may destroy certain elements of the host immune system (for example, HIV-1 infection may kill many TH cells, causing acquired severe combined immunodeficiency).

Direct or indirect cell death following viral infection contributes to disease signs of various severity. Loss of a few critical neurons in the brain may cause big damage (such as blindness or hearing loss). The severity of the disease depends on many factors, including (a) the number of viruses entering the host body, (b) the genetic nature of the virus, (c) the condition of the host (age, sex, immune status, pre-existing conditions, and genotype of the person), and (d) the port of entry of the virus.

Mild disease signs become apparent during the prodrome period of an infection (see Chapter 12). The infected person may transmit viruses to other individuals during the prodrome and the clinical illness that follows. All disease signs, including virus-specific disease signs, appear during the period of clinical illness (see Chapter 12). Many viral species may produce similar disease signs; thus, identifying a virus based on disease signs is difficult. Some common disease signs for viral infections are summarized in Table 11.4.

blocks.text: Unlike viruses, bacteria do not need to be inside the host body or cells to cause disease; the presence of bacterial endotoxins or exotoxins may be sufficient for bacterial pathogenesis. For example, a person would develop botulism (i.e., flaccid paralysis) by ingesting food contaminated with botulinum toxin, without coming in direct contact with Clostridium botulinum, the bacterium that produces the toxin. A person would develop a high fever if injected with a saline solution contaminated with bacterial endotoxins such as LPS.

Resident bacteria do not cause disease in healthy subjects as long as they occupy the allowable human body surfaces. Disease signs may appear if resident bacteria enter and grow in restricted body compartments, or if pathogenic bacteria colonize or disseminate within the human body. The pathogenesis of diseases caused by bacterial infections generally involves the following steps: (i) entrance to the body, (ii) adhesion to the body surfaces, (iii) colonization of certain body surfaces without causing disease for the time being (see Box 11.1), (iv) evasion of the innate and in some cases, adaptive immune responses of the body, (v) invasion of the immune surveillance and entering into the deeper tissues of the body, and (vi) destruction of tissues and organs (Fig. 11.6).

Box 11.1: Colonization, infection, and occupation Colonization is defined as the reproduction of microorganisms on the surfaces of a host’s body without causing tissue damage or clinical signs of disease. An infection is colonization by primary pathogens. A primary pathogen typically causes disease upon colonization, although there are exceptions. For instance, the upper respiratory tract of approximately 35.7% of healthy Japanese individuals is colonized by Staphylococcus aureus, a primary pathogen. Infections that do not involve tissue damage or clinical symptoms are referred to as inapparent or latent infections. Colonization of specific body surfaces such as the skin, mouth, upper respiratory tract, eyelids, cornea, outer and middle ear, alimentary canal, lower urethra, and vagina by normal microbiota is considered colonization (we will call it occupation). The normal microbiota found in any area of the body other than those listed above constitutes an opportunistic or secondary infection. Therefore, Staphylococcus epidermidis, which is part of the normal biota of the skin, becomes an opportunistic or secondary pathogen if it colonizes the endocardium of the heart. The six steps listed above can be performed in different sequences, and some of the steps can be combined or skipped for certain bacterial pathogens. The virulence factors of pathogenic bacteria, such as glycocalyx, flagella, pili, endotoxins, exotoxins, and some other metabolites (such as siderophores), help pathogens achieve one or more of the six objectives above. Resident and other opportunistic environmental bacteria may cause disease by taking some of the above steps, but only if the host’s immune mechanism is somewhat compromised.
Resident bacteria and the majority of environmental bacteria usually do not cause diseases for the following reasons: • They cannot grow or grow very slowly at body temperature.
• They do not invade the sterile tissues.
• They lack highly potent virulence factors, and they do not produce metabolites harmful to humans. • The immune system efficiently eliminates them from the body’s sterile spaces.
• The immune system quickly removes their harmful metabolites.

Any bacterial species, including resident and environmental ones such as Lactobacillus lactis, may cause opportunistic infections in subjects with a weakened immune system. However, some of the resident species, such as Enterobacter faecium are more aggressive opportunists than others (such as Lactobacillus lactis). Ironically, opportunistic infections caused by resident bacteria (such as Enterococcus faecalis) and environmental bacteria (such as Clostridioides difficile) are among the most difficult to treat.

blocks.text: Bacterial entrance in host body

Bacteria may enter the human body vertically from mother to child (through the placenta, during parturition, or through breastfeeding) and laterally through casual or sexual contacts, from aerosols, respiratory droplets, body fluids, and dander of other humans and animals, from inanimate substances (dust, dirt, fomites, and contaminated food and drinks), and through contaminated medical devices (see Chapter 12). Some pathogenic bacteria (for example, species of the genera Borrelia and Rickettsia) enter the human body through bites inflicted by their insect vectors. Intact skin, bordered by dead epithelial cells, is a highly protective barrier against infection. Only a few species of bacteria (including the spirochete Leptospira interrogans), may enter the body through the intact skin. Injured skin, however, is an effortless conduit of infection, where the entering bacteria directly enter deeper tissues and blood. Bacteria entering the body through animal bites also gain deeper access. Bacteria that come in contact with the mucous membrane face many immune defense mechanisms. Still, the mucous membranes are covered by live epithelial cells; the entering bacteria may find the mucous membranes more suitable (than skin) for the next steps of the infection process.
Bacterial adhesion to host cells and tissues

Unlike viruses, not all bacteria need biological receptors to adhere to body surfaces. For example, Streptococcus mutans may grow abundantly on human tooth surfaces, even though these surfaces are non-living and lack biological receptors. S. mutans adheres to the surface through its glycocalyx and creates a biofilm (see Box 11.2). Box 11.2: Biofilm A population of bacteria (of one or more species) secretes and shares capsular materials to form biofilms (Fig. 11.6). It is estimated that 60-80% of bacterial infections involve biofilms. A biofilm is a three- dimensional matrix composed of macromolecules (mostly polysaccharides, glycoproteins, and other proteins). Many bacterial species can rapidly develop biofilms on inanimate surfaces within the human body. Examples include exposed areas of tooth enamel, undigested food residues in the intestine, indwelling catheters, synthetic heart valves, prosthetic devices, pacemakers, intrauterine devices (IUDs) for birth control, and tampons inserted in the vagina. Environmental bacteria may produce biofilms on rocks, mud, the surfaces of aquatic plants and animals, and other substances. A biofilm is an organized community of bacteria. Despite the compact nature of a biofilm, bacteria within it can obtain adequate nutrients and readily remove metabolic wastes. Bacteria in biofilms are highly resistant to the body's immune response, chemotherapeutic agents, and many disinfectants. A dental plaque is a good example of a biofilm. Bacteria may form a biofilm on the wall of an indwelling catheter; a portion of the colony may break off and enter the bloodstream; the bacteria may then develop a biofilm on a synthetic heart valve. Numerous bacterial species (both primary pathogens and resident bacteria) form biofilms on implanted devices and dead tissues. Some species, for example Pseudomonas aeruginosa, may form biofilms on living tissues, including mucous membranes. It is estimated that about 5 million medical implants are used in the USA every year, and bacteria may develop biofilms on almost all types of medical implants. Bacterial biofilms are a persistent problem in modern medicine. In addition to bacteria, some species of protozoa and fungi form biofilms in both the environment and the patient's body. Biotechnologists are constantly seeking to develop physiologically acceptable implant materials inherently resistant to biofilm development. Primary pathogens generally use specific molecules (as ligands) to bind receptors on host cells. Bacterial ligands that bind to host cell receptors are collectively called adhesins. Genetic and biochemical studies have revealed many bacterial surface molecules that are adhesins. A few bacterial adhesins and host cell receptors with which they interact are listed in Table 11.6. Receptors for many bacterial adhesins are not fully elucidated.

Adhesion is generally an essential step in colonization or infection. If all the receptors of the epithelial cells of the mucous membrane were bound to the ligands of the resident microbiota, an entering foreign bacterium would be unable to adhere to the surface. The resident microbiota also synthesizes molecules that prevent invading microbes from colonizing these spaces. For example, lactobacilli synthesize acids and make the mucous membrane of the vagina unsuitable for fungal growth. If the normal microbiota is disrupted (for example, by antibiotic therapy), external pathogens would find ample receptors to interact with. The environmental bacterium Clostridioides difficile, for example, infects the large intestine only if the normal biota there is disrupted by prolonged antibiotic therapy. Bacterial invasion in host tissues Bacteria that enter the body through injuries can readily enter sterile tissues and blood. Some pathogenic bacteria may colonize the mucous membranes before damaging them and invading the submucosa (the tissue layer beneath the mucous membranes) to infect deeper tissues (Fig. 11.7). These pathogens produce various enzymes, exotoxins, and gases that facilitate their invasion of tissues. The molecules that help bacteria invade host tissues are grouped into invasins (proteins on the surface of live bacterial cells) and spreading factors (proteins and enzymes secreted by bacteria). Some important invasins and spreading factors and their functions are listed in Table 11.7.

Bacterial evasion of the host immune surveillance Bacterial pathogens must either withstand or, preferably, disable the host’s immune mechanisms to persist in the body and continue causing damage. Pathogenic bacteria employ various strategies to evade humoral (i.e., antibody-, complement-, and cytokine-mediated) and cell-mediated immune responses. Some common strategies bacteria use to evade host immune surveillance are listed in Table 11.8.
Destruction

Pathogenic bacteria destroy host molecules, cells, and tissues in diverse ways. Some bacterial products involved in adhesion, invasion, and evasion (described in the previous sections) also contribute to the destruction of host tissues. For example, bacterial hyaluronidase and collagenase (spreading factors) degrade tissue integrity, bacterial lipases degrade host cell membranes, and bacterial pore-forming toxins disrupt host cell membranes. Gases produced by Clostridium perfringens rupture host connective tissues. In the following sections, we will discuss bacterial toxins and how they damage host cells, tissues, and organs.
Bacterial Toxins
Toxins are harmful chemical substances produced by the metabolic activities of certain organisms. Bacterial toxins can be divided into two major categories: endotoxins and exotoxins.
Bacterial endotoxins

Endotoxins are cell-associated toxins. Because they are integral parts of bacterial cells, they can be released only after death. The principal endotoxins are lipopolysaccharides (LPS) found in the outer membrane of G(-) bacteria. Other bacterial molecules with endotoxin-like activities include the bacterial peptidoglycan cell wall, lipoteichoic acids (LTA) of G(+) bacteria, arabinogalactan and mycolic acids of actinobacteria, and bacterial RNA and DNA. All of these are non-protein molecules, so they are heat-stable (boiling does not destroy these agents). Endotoxins act by binding TLR or some other receptors on the host cell surface (see Chapter 9). Receptor binding activates powerful signal transduction pathways, leading to the expression of new proteins, including pro- inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha (Fig. 11.9).

If many dead bacteria are present in the host body (as in sepsis), many leukocytes would be activated, leading to the secretion of excessive inflammatory cytokines. This process, collectively called the pyrogenic acute response (also known as cytokine storm), includes fever, vasodilation, blood clotting, activation of complement pathways, and rapid/devastating hypotension (vascular shock), which can be fatal. Unlike LPS, peptidoglycan and LTA induce a modest pyrogenic acute response. Bacterial exotoxins Exotoxins are proteins secreted by toxigenic strains of pathogenic bacteria. Most, but not all, exotoxins are heat-labile (inactivated by boiling). Exotoxins can be divided into three categories: Type I, Type II, and Type III, as described below (also see Table 11.9).
Type I exotoxins

Type I exotoxins bind receptors on the host cell and activate a signal transduction pathway. Type I exotoxins do not damage the host cell membrane and do not enter the host cell. A good example of type I toxins is superantigens secreted by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes. The superantigens simultaneously bind to the TCRs on TH cells and the MHC II molecules on antigen-presenting cells, such as macrophages, activating TH cells. Activated TH cells secrete excessive cytokines, which may lead to vascular shock (Fig. 11.10).
Type II exotoxins

Type II exotoxins are membrane-active proteins, such as leucocidins and hemolysins, secreted by Staphylococcus aureus. These toxins damage the membrane by forming pores, which kill the affected host cells (Fig. 11.10).

Cytokines activate the immune system to eradicate pathogens, but they may also cause many of the disease signs associated with bacterial infections.
Type III exotoxins

Type III exotoxins are secreted toxins that usually act after entering the host cell. Many members of this family of exotoxins are made of A and B components. They usually have an A1-B1 or A1-B5 subunit combination (Fig. 11.10). Usually, the B subunit binds the receptor present in the host cells and helps the A subunit to enter the host cell. The A subunit, and in some cases both A and B subunits, subsequently carry out the damaging biological activities. The outcomes (i.e., the detrimental effects) are diverse (Table 11.9), including signal transduction and activation of certain enzymes; inhibition of endosomal movement within the host cell; alteration of certain structural components of the host cell; deregulation of membrane channels; and inhibition of protein synthesis.

Destruction due to immunopathology in bacterial infections The immune responses to bacterial (or other microbial) infections lead to significant morbidity and, in some cases, mortality. Here are some of the pathologies the immune system contributes to in response to bacterial infections. Damages due to cytokine storm During bacterial sepsis (growth of bacteria in the blood and visceral organs), bacterial endotoxins, especially LPS of G(-) bacteria in the blood (and other body fluids) bind TLRs and other receptors, activating macrophages. The macrophages release massive amounts of cytokines that lead to (a) excess cytokine secretion by various leukocytes, (b) unregulated complement activation and tissue damage, (c) uncontrolled blood clotting, (d) high fever, (e) vascular shock (extremely low blood pressure), and (f) multiple organ failure. Bacterial sepsis is usually fatal unless treated in a critical care facility. Some exotoxins, such as TSST-1 superantigens of Staphylococcus aureus) may also trigger a cytokine storm and vascular shock by locking TH cells onto antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages (Fig. 11.10). In this case, the cytokines are released by activated TH cells, but the ultimate outcome is the same as in sepsis. Damage by antibodies Type II hypersensitivity reactions Some bacteria (such as S. aureus, Treponema pallidum, and Campylobacter jejune) secrete bacterial molecules that are structurally similar to some host proteins. Antibodies specific to those bacterial antigens may cross-react with (thus bind) the antigens on the host cells. Such binding activates complement pathways and neutrophils, leading to inflammation and tissue damage. Heart muscle damage (myocarditis) and joint pain (rheumatic arthritis) after S. aureus infection and Guillain-Barré Syndrome (paralysis due to nerve damage) after Campylobacter jejuni infections are Type II hypersensitivity reactions (see Chapter 9).
Type III hypersensitivity reactions

People infected with certain strains of Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Borrelia burgdorferi synthesize non-neutralizing IgG antibodies that bind bacterial antigens and form immune (i.e., antigen-antibody) complexes (see Chapter 9). The immune complexes may settle in narrow blood vessels and activate the complement pathway. Depending on the tissues in which immune complexes deposit, disease symptoms can include skin damage, kidney failure, joint pain, and even paralysis.

Damage by leucocytes Inflammation Microbial infection activates neutrophils and macrophages. Activated macrophages secrete various inflammatory cytokines (including IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha) and activate TH cells. Activated TH cells secrete additional cytokines, and the cascade generates a massive inflammatory response.

Some signs of inflammation include pain, low-grade fever, chills, night sweats, fatigue, sleeplessness, weight loss, nausea, diarrhea, atherosclerosis (buildup of lipid plaques in the arteries), lymphadenopathy (swelling of the lymph nodes), and hepatosplenomegaly (enlargement of the liver and spleen).

Chronic infections may lead to chronic inflammation, with less severe signs of disease. However, prolonged chronic inflammation may also cause additional damage. For example, chronic inflammation due to chronic infection of the stomach by Helicobacter pylori may lead to stomach cancer.

Diseases such as bacterial meningitis (inflammation of the membranes that cover the brain) are primarily driven by cell-mediated inflammatory responses rather than by bacterial tissue damage. Bacteria generally cannot enter the brain or the meninges because of the blood-brain barrier (created by the endothelial cells of the brain's blood vessels). Inflammation triggered by the bacterial antigens may cause vasodilation, allowing bacteria to enter the meninges. The presence of bacteria in the meninges activates macrophages. Activated macrophages destroy tissues containing bacteria or their antigens, which leads to meningitis.

Blindness caused by Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae is not due to bacterial damage to the retina. Instead, the bacteria and their antigens activate neutrophils and macrophages. Activated leucocytes damage the eyelid tissue and cause scarring. The scar tissue of the eyelids rubs against the cornea. Over time, the cornea becomes opaque, leading to blindness.
Type IV hypersensitivity reactions

When macrophages fail to kill phagocytized bacteria (such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis), the infected cells secrete cytokines that activate TH cells. The activated TH cells also secrete additional cytokines. As a result, millions of macrophages, cytotoxic T cells, neutrophils, eosinophils, and fibroblasts surround the infected macrophages, forming a granuloma or tubercle (Fig. 11.11).
Fig. 11.11. Granulomas in chronic granulomatous diseases. A. Genesis of a granuloma. Macrophages and dendritic

cells persistently infected by bacteria present bacterial antigens to T cells. They also secrete cytokines and chemokines. Many leucocytes migrate to the site and create a granuloma around the infected macrophages or DCs, damaging nearby tissues and blood vessels. Lack of oxygen causes cell death and necrosis. B. A granuloma with a necrotic center from the lung of a tuberculosis patient. Image-Wikipedia.

In granulomas, macrophages reorganize into an epithelial cell-like structure and fuse to form giant cells. As the granuloma grows larger (due to the accumulation of additional leukocytes around the initial granuloma), it damages local blood vessels and other structures, such as the alveoli of the lung. Ultimately, the granuloma becomes fibrous, and the cells in the core die by necrosis (due to a lack of oxygen supply). The bacteria inside the granuloma may enter latency or form a biofilm. On occasion, the host immune system may resolve the granuloma and restore healthy tissue, but more often, the encased bacteria remain viable and may activate it and even break it open. Reinfection by the same bacteria may exacerbate granuloma formation. Granulomas are hallmarks of tuberculosis and leprosy. The effects of bacterial infections of the organ systems are discussed further in Chapters 12-14.

blocks.text: Fungi may cause multiple human diseases, including intoxication, allergies, inflammations, and tissue destruction.

Food and drinks contaminated with mycotoxins (fungal toxins) are sources of intoxication. Mycotoxins pose major challenges in animal husbandry. These toxins can accumulate in animal meat and milk and pass to human consumers. Some fungal toxins that may affect humans are shown in Table 11.10. The table indicates that potent toxins can be easily avoided in developed countries, where high-quality, inspected food is abundant. However, in hot, humid developing countries, where fungi thrive, it is challenging to completely prevent citizens from being exposed to mycotoxins. Avoiding fungus-contaminated items, especially peanuts and products made with peanut butter or peanut oil, cereals, wine, spices, herbal medications, and herbal teas imported from developing countries may help reduce exposure to mycotoxins.

Fungal infections (or mycoses) are more common among immunocompromised and debilitated individuals. Major contributors to fungal pathogenesis include tissue damage (caused by fungal proteases), physical interference (from hyphae and mycelia within tissues), fungal metabolites, and the host’s inflammatory response to fungal antigens. Various fungal species can infect the same tissue and produce similar disease symptoms. It is important to note that the occurrence and severity of fungal infections largely depend on the patient's condition (Table 11.11). Some fungi are endemic, affecting only local populations, while occupation also plays a significant role in contracting mycoses.
Table 11.11. Predisposing factors for mycoses.
Factors Susceptible groups Age Low birth-weight babies, infants, and the elderly.
Sex Females, especially pregnant women and premature female children (exception-males more susceptible than females to Histoplasma capsulatum).
Occupation Soil and bird-dropping movers, grave diggers, cleaners, gardeners, farmers, animal handlers, pet owners, and cave explorers (exposure to bat droppings).

Injuries Burns, traumatic injuries, surgical wounds, indwelling catheters, and prostheses use. Drug use Corticosteroids, birth control pills, broad-spectrum antibiotics, intravenous drug abuse. Immune system status Low neutrophil count, chronic granulomatous disease, poor cell-mediated immunity. Living conditions Certain geographic areas, hot and humid weather, houses with leaky roofs and walls, crowded conditions, dusty bedrooms, and wet linens.

Virulence factors of fungi Ability to grow at 37°C Most fungi typically thrive in the cooler temperatures of shady environments (15-30°C). Many fungi grow very slowly or not at all at 37°C. The host immune system readily eliminates slow-growing fungi from the body. The ability to grow at 37°C is a distinguishing characteristic of primary fungal pathogens and a few opportunistic ones. Dimorphism People are exposed to fungal spores more often than to mold and yeast. The host immune system quickly removes spores, but a few may germinate in wounds and the lungs. Most pathogenic fungi are dimorphic, exhibiting both mold and yeast growth stages. This morphological transition also causes changes in their surface antigens. The surface antigens of mold and yeast forms may differ, and this difference can help fungi evade host immune surveillance. Cell wall components The yeast form of virulent fungal strains possesses a thick layer of beta (1,3)-glucan in the cell wall. The yeast form often sheds protein antigens (such as the WI-1 antigen of Blastomyces sp.) from the cell wall into the host body. The soluble protein antigens bind to antibodies, thereby preventing antibody deposition on the fungal cell wall. Interference with the host immune system Some pathogenic fungi (such as Blastomyces sp.) prevent phagocytosis, while some (such as Coccidioides sp.) allow phagocytosis but prevent phagocytic killing. While T cell-mediated immunity (TH1-type immunity) is necessary for fighting fungal infections, most fungi suppress T cell immunity and increase antibody production (TH2-type immunity), which is ineffective against them.
Enzymes and secondary metabolites

Many fungi (such as the genera Coccidioides, Candida, and Aspergillus) secrete enzymes that digest host collagen, elastin, and other fibrous tissues. A few pathogenic fungi (such as Aspergillus sp.) secrete gliotoxins in the infected tissue, which suppress the host immune response. Cryptococcus neoformans secretes melanin, a pigment that inhibits phagocytosis and phagocytic killing.
Pathology due to inflammatory responses

Fungal molecules (such as glycoproteins and polysaccharides) bind to TLRs and other receptors, activating leukocytes. Activated leukocytes secrete cytokines and also damage affected tissues, inducing disease symptoms such as skin damage, nodules, and fungal balls in the lungs, asthma, and delayed-type (type IV) hypersensitivity. Allergies Allergies develop if IgE antibodies are produced in response to fungal antigens. Chronic exposure to fungal spores can lead to various allergic conditions of the skin, eyes, lungs, and other organs. Living in old houses with water leakage problems is a significant contributing factor to fungal allergies. The most effective way to avoid fungal allergies is to eliminate fungi from living spaces.
The effects of fungal infections on organ systems are further discussed in Chapters 13-15.

blocks.text: The pathogenesis of eukaryotic microbes has not been investigated as extensively as that of viruses and bacteria. The mechanism of protozoan pathogenesis is cryptically presented here.
Adherence, entrance, and replication

Protozoa that infect the intestine are acquired through contaminated water and food. Almost all intestinal (and a few blood) protozoa form cysts, which are stable in the environment. Human and animal feces are significant sources of protozoan cysts. Fecal-oral contact (hand-to-food and hand-to-mouth) and undercooked animal flesh are important contributors to the transmission of cysts as well as vegetative cells. A few species of protozoa colonize the genital tract. These species are typically transmitted through sexual contact and, to a lesser extent, by fomites (inanimate objects such as cloths). Animal vectors (ticks, mosquitoes, flies, and other insects) transmit blood protozoa. Some protozoa remain in the lumen of the gut, genital tract, or blood vessels, loosely attached to nearby host cells. Others enter host cells, reproduce there, and ultimately damage the cell (Table 11.12). Like bacteria, protozoa adhere to host cells via adhesins, molecules that bind to host-cell receptors. For example, the malarial parasite binds to the Duffy blood group antigen on erythrocytes. The presence of such receptors determines the tissue tropism of protozoa. Tissue and cell damage Protozoan pathogens may secrete various proteases and lipases that can degrade host proteins and lipids, respectively. For example, Entamoeba histolytica secretes proteases that degrade the intestinal mucosa. Intracellular protozoa (such as the malarial parasite) produce toxic metabolic byproducts such as hemozoin in infected erythrocytes. When the infected cells break open, the toxic metabolites cause fever and chills and activate T cells.

Intestinal protozoa typically cause diarrhea by damaging the mucous membrane and activating leukocytes. Common problems associated with diarrhea include dehydration and reduced nutrient absorption. Malabsorption weakens the infected person and makes them vulnerable to secondary bacterial and fungal infections.

As with any other microbes, protozoan infections activate the immune system. Infection by Trypanosomes, for example, may trigger any of the four types of hypersensitivity reactions. Parasitic infections and cell damage also stimulate macrophages and TH cells to release cytokines, leading to high fever and other disease symptoms. Meningitis caused by protozoan parasites primarily results from leukocyte-induced inflammation in the affected tissues.
Table 11.12. How protozoa cause disease (shown schematically).

Diarrhea, malabsorption Intestinal protozoa (genera Entamoeba, Isospora, and Cyclospora, for example). How protozoa avoid the host immune response Protozoan parasites are removed from the body mainly by (a) Complement activation by the classical (antibody-dependent) pathway.
(b) Phagocytic killing (c) Leucocytes kill infected cells through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) (d) TC cells kill infected human cells.

Most protozoan parasites are highly adapted to evade host immune responses. Some blood protozoa infect erythrocytes, so host antibodies may not bind the parasites effectively. Trypanosomes frequently alter surface antigens (antigenic variation), so previously induced antibodies may not recognize the mutated antigens. Some protozoa escape the phagosome of a macrophage and migrate to the cytoplasm. Other parasites remain within the phagosome and prevent phagolysosome formation, thereby avoiding destruction. Malarial parasites induce immunosuppression through mechanisms not fully elucidated. A high load of parasite antigens in the host body may induce tolerance to the pathogen.
Intoxication

Diatoms and dinoflagellates do not infect humans. However, these organisms produce toxins under certain environmental conditions. The toxins accumulate in filter-feeding shellfish (such as oysters) without causing noticeable harm to the organisms. Humans can suffer from intoxication by consuming the affected shellfish. Several species of cyanobacteria also produce toxins, and in rare cases, these toxins may reach humans through fish and shellfish. The common algal toxins are listed in Table 11.13. Human neurological diseases caused by algal toxins are generally referred to as paralytic fish poisoning.

blocks.text: Unlike bacteria and protozoa, the offspring of worms typically do not infect the same host unless the fertilized eggs or embryos leave the host and re-enter the body through an appropriate port of entry. Mechanisms of helminth pathogenesis differ by species. In all cases, the eggs or larvae must enter the patient's body, the worms must survive, and, in some instances, reproduce inside the victim's body to cause disease syndromes. The following is a general description of the pathogenesis processes.

Adherence, entrance, movement, and reproduction Eggs and encysted worms can enter the human body through food and beverages. In rare cases, infections may result from inhaling airborne worm eggs or consuming/accidentally inhaling worm-infected insects and water fleas. Worm cysts and eggs may contain tiny hooks, suckers, or mucous plugs that help them adhere to the victim's body (Table 11.14). The cysts of certain flukes are strategically placed (on aquatic plants, within insect body cavities, and in the muscle tissues of animals) to facilitate transfer to the next host. Larvae of filarial worms and some other worms enter the body through insect bites. Free-living aquatic or soil larvae of some worms may penetrate the human body from water and soil through openings created by the larvae in the victim's skin.

Because skin is covered by dead cells, receptor-mediated adherence is not a viable option for worm larvae to attach to human skin. Worm larvae typically have various glands that secrete enzymes to digest the host's skin and tissue matrices. They may migrate from the skin to nearby blood vessels, and from the blood vessels to various organs, including the lungs, liver, brain, eyes, and spinal cord. Larvae of some species move from the intestine to the body cavity (i.e., coelom) and then to the liver; they also move from the lungs to the airways and throat, where they may be swallowed with sputum and occupy the intestine.

Most flatworms are hermaphrodites, and a hermaphrodite flatworm's sperm can fertilize its own eggs, resulting in the release of hundreds or even thousands of eggs daily. However, sexual union between two hermaphrodite worms is also common. Blood flukes are not hermaphrodites; the male blood flukes permanently clasp the females to ensure sexual reproduction. Most roundworms are unisexual, so the sexual union of male and female roundworms is necessary for egg fertilization.
Table 11.14. Some common strategies worms employ for infecting their victims.

Strategies How the strategies work Adhesive properties Eggs are highly sticky (example, eggs of Ascaris sp.), larvae may have hooks and suckers to adhere to the host animals (example flukes) Ability of digging holes in tissues Larvae have glands that secrete lytic enzymes to make holes in the tissues, so the worm may migrate (i.e. move through) the tissue masses.

Eggs and larvae in the food Eggs, cysts and larvae are stable in the moist environments; eggs and larvae present in soiled fruits and vegetables and in flesh and organs of the food animals for easy delivery of the larvae and eggs to the host organisms.

Ability to survive stomach acid Eggs, cysts and larvae eaten through food may survive stomach acid Reproductive specialties Worms lay a very large number of eggs; asexual and hermaphrodite reproduction ensure reproductive success. Some unisexual male and female worms tie for the lifetime to ensure reproductive success.

Ability to utilize intermediate/ alternative hosts as the vectors Biting insects may deliver worm larvae directly to host blood, infected insects and water flea can be eaten or accidentally inhaled. Roundworms may infect many different vertebrate species (lack host restriction).

Ability to survive in tissues and blood Egg, larvae and adult worms may survive on solid tissues (such as muscles) mucous membranes and blood, despite of the presence of diverse immune defenses there.
Tissue and cell damage

The migration of larvae through organs—especially the skin, intestine, liver, and eye—induces inflammation, sometimes severely. Guinea worms cause necrotic skin sores. Onchocerca volvulus (the eye worm) can cause significant skin damage and blindness. Hookworms bite into and invade the intestinal mucosa and suck host blood. Excessive hookworm infection may lead to anemia. The migration of a large number of Trichinella sp. larvae (from ingested uncooked or undercooked meat) across the host’s intestine may cause severe tissue damage and can be fatal. It is suspected that lost explorers from Andree’s North Pole Expedition (1897) consumed raw bear meat and died from intestinal injuries caused by migrating worms (especially Trichinella sp.).

High fever and certain anthelminthic drugs may trigger a rapid migration of intestinal worms, particularly Ascaris lumbricoides. The migrating worms may penetrate the intestinal wall, bile duct, and pancreatic duct. Leakage into the intestine encourages bacterial growth in the body cavities, which, if not treated, almost always leads to fatal septicemia. Obstruction or leakage in the bile and pancreatic ducts, along with the inflammatory responses to these events, could have severe or even fatal consequences.

Liver fluke infections cause significant liver damage and hepatomegaly. Inflammation caused by worm infections can lead to cell damage, resulting in fatty degeneration (excess fat accumulation in the cell), necrosis (cell lysis), hyperplasia (cell proliferation), hypertrophy (increase in organ size), and metaplasia (the change of one type of cell in an organ to another type of cell due to changes in the gene expression program). The inflammatory response induced by eggs of blood flukes (Schistosoma sp.) deposited in the bladder and prostate, and by liver flukes (Fasciola hepatica) occupying the bile ducts, may lead to cancers.
Physical blockage and pressure

Eggs of flatworms and larvae of nematodes can obstruct smaller blood vessels. Such blockages in the brain (Fig. 11.12), compounded by inflammatory responses, may lead to severe neurological symptoms. The blockage of lymph vessels by filarial worms results in massive hypertrophy, known as elephantiasis, in the limbs (Fig. 11.12) and genitalia. Intestinal worms, particularly Ascaris sp., can physically obstruct the intestine and block the passage of gut contents. Large hydatid cysts in solid organs, such as the liver and brain (Fig. 11.12), can create pressure that damages nearby tissues.
Loss of nutrients and malabsorption

A few dozen hookworms may consume enough blood from a host to cause anemia. Many intestinal worms rely almost exclusively on glucose for nutrition. Because worms produce ATP primarily through glycolysis, the parasite must absorb a significant amount of glucose from the host. As a result, a heavily infected person may lose some food calories to the worms. For this and other reasons, subjects heavily infected with intestinal worms may consume a high- calorie diet without gaining weight. Worm infections can lead to loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting (due to inflammatory responses), and malabsorption.
Fig. 11.12. Some pathologies related to worm infections. A. Elephantiasis. Microscopic filarial worms block the

lymph vessels and hinder lymph flow. New lymph vessels grow around the blockage to compensate, leading to tissue hypertrophy (i.e., elephantiasis). B. An MRI image of a person’s brain displaying worm (Taenia solium) cysts (indicated by the arrows). Similar cysts can develop in muscles and other organs. C. A gross pathology photograph of hydatid cysts excised from the lung of an infected subject, which contain many larvae. Such cysts may also grow in the liver, bones, and brain. Images from CDC-PHIL.

Inflammation and the disruption in the host immune system Female pinworms (Enterobius vermicularis) inhabit the colon but migrate to the rectum to lay their eggs. This migration triggers a severe inflammatory response. Injuries to the eye, skin, liver, bladder, brain, and muscle caused by worm infections are primarily inflammatory in origin. A significant number of muscle cells die around the encysted muscle worms (i.e., Trichinella sp.). The presence of worm cysts in fine muscles can completely disable the muscles. For instance, individuals with worms in the eye muscles cannot move their eyes. Neutrophils, macrophages, eosinophils, and T cells are activated during the early phase of worm infection. An increase in eosinophil count (i.e., eosinophilia) is regarded as an indication of worm infection. Activated leukocytes secrete cytokines, leading to both local and systemic inflammation. Common mechanisms of pathologies caused by worm infection are summarized in
Table 11.15.
Table 11.15. Mechanisms of pathology due to worm infections.
Type 	Example

Enzymatic damage Enzymes secreted by the larval glands damage skin and some connective tissues. Direct tissue damage Movement of the adult worms or larvae through the tissues and organs may cause internal bleeding and induce inflammation.

Blockage of various ducts Intestinal worms may block the intestinal lumen; filarial worms block the lumen of the lymph vessels; liver worms may block the bile ducts, and worm eggs may block fine blood vessels of the brain and other organs.

Immunopathology Type I hypersensitivity Type II hypersensitivity Type III hypersensitivity Examples Inflammation of the lung after lung fluke infections Tissue and kidney damage after Schistosoma sp. infection Tissue damage after Schistosoma sp. infection Tissue damage Fatty degeneration and hepatomegaly (swelling of the liver) due to liver fluke infection.

How worms avoid and disrupt the host immune response The role of the immune system in worm infections is poorly understood. Healthy individuals exhibit fewer signs of worm infections, whereas immunocompromised individuals suffer from severe diseases, demonstrating that an intact immune system is essential in combating worm infections. Worms, along with their eggs and larvae, induce both cellular and humoral immune responses. Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC)-mediated killing by granulocytes and mast cell degranulation (Fig. 11.13) are primary immune effector mechanisms against worms and their larvae.
Fig 11.13. The major immune responses to worm infections and how worms evade effector mechanisms. A.

Mast cells degranulate when they interact with IgE deposited on the surface of the parasite. This inflammatory process attracts other leukocytes to the site. B cells secrete antibodies (IgE and IgG) that bind to parasite antigens. Activated TH cells (typically Th2-type cells) release cytokines that activate macrophages and B cells to secrete more IgG and IgE antibodies. ADCC by macrophages, eosinophils, and neutrophils may lead to the parasite's death. Some methods parasites use to evade host immune responses are indicated below the worm.

Worms have evolved exquisitely to avoid host immune responses. They possess a very tough cuticle, which host proteolytic enzymes may not be able to destroy. Some worms secrete enzymes that digest antibodies deposited on their cuticle. Schistosoma sp. periodically changes the antigens on its cuticle or expresses antigens that mimic some of the host's antigens. Such antigenic variation and mimicry prevent antibodies and suppress effective B cell activation. Schistosoma sp. masks its surface with host proteins, such as Fc receptors, to prevent antibody deposition. The worms and their motile larvae may move away from leukocyte aggregates to evade killing through ADCC. Some worms, worm eggs, and larvae form granulomas due to the accumulation of leukocytes around them. The granuloma (also called a cyst) may become fibrous due to the activities of fibroblasts. The core of the granuloma can become necrotic due to toxic substances secreted by the leukocytes or the parasite itself. Such granulomas are called palisading granulomas, and the parasites may remain unharmed within them.

sections.heading: Some commonsense ways to prevent microbial infections

blocks.text: Good hygiene practices, personal protective measures, lifestyle choices, and public health safety measures (Table 11.16) greatly influence the frequency of microbial infections.
Table 11.16. Common measures that are preventive to virus infections (the list is not exhaustive).
Measure 	Major steps
Personal hygiene Proper handwashing after touching any surface that is actually or potentially contaminated by microbes.
Personal protection Obtaining proper training for handling biohazard materials, wearing proper garb, laboratory goggles, double gloves, face mask, and respirator whenever applicable.
Lifestyle choices Avoiding recreational (injectable) drug use, casual sexual activities, extra caution on tattooing, mutilation, and body piercing.
Avoiding potentially contaminated food (raw animal meat, unpasteurized milk, and cheese), and direct contact with contaminated dirt, warm water pools, and wild and pet animals.

Public health measures Enforcing childhood vaccination, proper inspection of food (eggs, seafood, meat, poultry, fruits, and vegetables), proper vaccination of pets (and, if feasible, wild animals), controlling mosquitoes, ticks, and other vectors, postmortem inspection of deceased wild animals, and epidemiological surveillance.
